items.title: [phys.org] Researchers document sustained sexual bond between Ethiopian bull and male donkey
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

An Italian-led research team documented repeated sexual interactions between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau, describing a selective social bond between the animals. During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology. The pair also licked, rubbed and nuzzled one another, and researchers repeatedly saw them seek each other out despite access to other potential mates. The team cautions that observations of one domesticated pair cannot establish why the behavior occurred or what the animals felt. Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Oklahoma will prohibit data centers from using groundwater for evaporative cooling starting Nov. 1, requiring closed-loop or immersion systems under a new law. The restriction applies to water use inside facilities, but electricity generation can account for a larger share of data centers’ water footprint. The law follows drought conditions in western Oklahoma during much of 2026; Pennsylvania has separately required data centers using more than 10 megawatts to disclose energy and water use. Forbes cited national figures showing that power plants serving data centers consumed far more water in 2023 than data centers used for cooling.

items.title: [efeagro.com] Hackers raise supermarket freezer temperatures across Europe, spoiling food
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration at grocery stores and other businesses in several European countries overnight into Nov. 2, raising temperatures in some units to 50°C and prompting businesses to discard food or remove it as a precaution. Affected countries included Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg; reports also described incidents in Italy, though the extent there remains unclear. In Belgium, Delhaize reported refrigeration problems in about 40 stores, Carrefour in 15 and Spar in five. Ireland’s SuperValu reported incidents at 13 stores, while refrigeration supplier Danfoss said at least 17 Dutch businesses were affected. The attackers appear to have remotely changed settings on connected equipment, in some cases activating defrost mode. European Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described the repeated attacks as an attempt to disrupt food supply and weaken consumer trust, but said food security was not currently threatened. Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation, but no group has claimed responsibility and authorities have not established whether the incidents were part of one operation. Italy scheduled a government crisis meeting for Nov. 3 with national cybersecurity and intelligence officials.

items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [thehindu.com] Russia and Ukraine agree to Oleshky truce for aid and evacuations
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Russia and Ukraine have agreed to pause fighting around Russian-occupied Oleshky in southern Ukraine to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations under an arrangement brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, officials said Friday. Russia’s military chief and Ukraine’s General Staff said their forces would stop firing at 4 a.m. Moscow time on Oct. 27. The White House had announced Oct. 29 as the ceasefire’s start date, while Ukrainian negotiator Dmytro Lubinets, the country’s human rights ombudsman, said the humanitarian mission would begin on Oct. 29 and the pause would last several days. Oleshky’s population has fallen from about 24,000 before the invasion to an estimated 1,700-2,000, including about 50 children. Residents face shortages of food, medicine and clean water, limited electricity, mined roads and continuing military attacks. The first steps are expected to include assessing residents’ needs and clearing mines before aid convoys enter. Civilian teams are to coordinate transport for those choosing to leave for either Russia or Ukraine. The ceasefire is expected to cover the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation. Lubinets said it would last several days; officials have not provided details on how compliance will be monitored. Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said technical-level talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States are planned for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Canadian police suspend use of Crime Stoppers after 1.5 million records exposed
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Canadian police services are suspending their use of Crime Stoppers after a breach exposed more than 1.5 million tips submitted across Canada over 25 years, a CBC News investigation found. More than 850,000 records included personally identifiable information. The tips were managed through P3, software provided by U.S.-based Navigate360. Navigate360 acknowledged on Friday that its database had been breached between November 2025 and March 2026 and said potentially exposed information included names, addresses, birth dates and Social Security numbers. The company said it had no evidence the information had been used for fraud or identity theft. Police in several provinces have paused their use of the service while they assess the breach and its safeguards. Toronto and Ottawa police are directing people to report information through police channels, which do not necessarily offer the same anonymity. Crime Stoppers chapters and police are seeking further details from Navigate360. The company said it hired a cybersecurity firm to help strengthen security.

items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Russian strikes hit a school used to distribute humanitarian aid and a nearby shelter in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, on Nov. 2. Ukrainian officials initially reported at least 26 dead; regional administrator Mykhailo Semikin said Tuesday that the toll had risen to 29 as rescue work continued. Five people were reported injured, and officials said dozens were missing. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the school distributed aid every Monday and that a second wave of bombs hit people who had taken shelter after the initial strike. The attack followed the end of a six-day local truce in neighboring Kherson, arranged to allow aid deliveries and evacuations from Russian-occupied Oleshky. Kyiv accused Russian forces of using the pause to strengthen their positions; Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said adjusting positions during a ceasefire was normal and alleged Ukraine had done so too. U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. officials are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11. The working-level talks are set to address postwar security, de-escalation, humanitarian issues and further steps toward ending the war.

items.title: [discovermagazine.com] Tests find coca and alcohol in Inca child mummies, but none of the hallucinogens screened for
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Researchers analyzing hair and nails from eight Inca children sacrificed about 500 years ago found traces of coca in hair and evidence of alcohol in some children, but none of the hallucinogens they tested for. The remains came from mountain sites in Peru and Argentina and belonged to children aged 6 to 14. The findings suggest the substances may have helped prepare children for the physical and emotional strain of journeys to sacrificial sites rather than induce hallucinations, said archaeologist Dagmara Socha of the University of Warsaw. Harmine, a plant compound associated with Amazonian species, was found in a nail from Juanita, a 14-year-old mummy. The team plans further study of the substances and sacred mountain sites.

items.title: [abcnews.com] Swift telescope shutdown ends rapid alerts for cosmic explosions
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

NASA shut down its Swift Observatory in late October after it could no longer hold steady enough for observations, ending a 22-year mission to detect gamma-ray bursts, supernovas and other high-energy events. Swift’s rapid observations helped direct other space telescopes toward eruptions for more detailed study, and astronomers are working out how to replace that alert function. The observatory resumed observations after the rescue effort ended and captured additional gamma-ray bursts and other ultrahigh-energy events before NASA turned off its systems. Over its mission, Swift recorded more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars.
